orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the May 17, 2011 denial of summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: On October 31, 2007, plaintiff was working at Wilson’s Leather in the mall and slipped on a puddle in its back room caused by a ceiling leak. The opinion identifies Newburgh Capital as owner and Urban Retail as manager of Newburgh Mall; leaks had occurred elsewhere in the store for about three months.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants asserted noncreation, but the stated appellate analysis resolved constructive notice without a distinct creation finding.
Defendants asserted lack of actual notice; the opinion’s specific holding addresses constructive notice, not a separate actual-notice determination.

Defendants established lack of constructive notice of the particular ceiling leak; plaintiff supplied no sufficient duration showing. Leaks elsewhere in the store did not give constructive notice of the accident-causing leak.
Plaintiff’s evidence of leaks for roughly three months in a different part of the store did not establish notice of the particular defect; the court distinguished an unrelated/general problem.

quality.notes: The actual private retail back room and mall ownership/management description support control; the wording does not allocate legal title to each defendant or provide lease terms. owner/manager follows the stated mall roles collectively. Plaintiff was working at the store, but precise employee/contractor status and employer are unstated, so injured_role=other. The 2007 accident date does not exclude the 2012 opinion. No deposition, affidavit, photograph or maintenance-record format is specified. The three-month history concerns another part of the store and is not the duration of this leak.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.

This action arose from a slip-and-fall at one of the stores located at the defendant Newburgh Mall, LLC, which is owned by the defendant Newburgh Capital Group, LLC, and managed by the defendant Urban Retail Properties, LLC (hereinafter Urban Retail). On October 31, 2007, the plaintiff was working at a store known as Wilson’s Leather when she slipped and fell on a puddle in the store’s back room, which resulted from a leak in the store’s ceiling.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Dutchess County (Brands, J.), dated May 17, 2011, which denied their motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

The defendants moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint on the ground that they did not create the alleged dangerous condition, nor did they have actual or constructive notice of the alleged dangerous condition.

The defendants established their entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by making a prima facie showing that they did not have constructive notice of the alleged dangerous condition of the ceiling. In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact. There was no showing that the leak had existed for a sufficient period of time for the defendants to have acquired constructive notice
Moreover, although the plaintiff showed that there had been leaks in another part of the store for about three months,
Here, the leak in the other part of the store was insufficient to charge the defendants with constructive notice of the leak that caused the plaintiff to fall
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: On March 17, 2017, plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on ice in an exterior parking lot on premises owned by EFG and leased by Barnes & Noble Booksellers.

legal_issues.finding: EFG had no snow/ice-removal duty for the subject lot as an out-of-possession landlord; the opinion does not recite lease terms or assign every duty of the tenant.
Defendants established noncreation of the ice prima facie, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. The opinion does not detail the underlying proof.
Defendants established lack of actual notice prima facie, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. The opinion does not detail the underlying proof.
Defendants established lack of constructive notice prima facie, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. The opinion does not detail the underlying proof.
EFG additionally established that it was an out-of-possession landlord with no duty to remove snow/ice from this lot; plaintiff raised no triable issue.

quality.notes: Ownership and lease of the actual premises are express. parking_only records the stated setting without inferring bookstore use or plaintiff’s customer/employee status from the tenant’s name. No evidence formats, lease clauses, inspection details or storm facts are supplied. The separate EFG duty ground supplements the common noncreation/notice ground; it does not create multiple appealed orders or a mixed result. evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, without costs or disbursements.

On March 17, 2017, the plaintiff allegedly sustained injuries when he slipped and fell on ice in an exterior parking lot. The premises was owned by the defendant EFG & P, LLC (hereinafter EFG), and leased by the defendant Barnes & Noble Booksellers, Inc.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Richmond County (Judith N. McMahon, J.), dated July 23, 2020. The order granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Here, the defendants established, prima facie, that they did not create the alleged ice condition or have actual or constructive notice of its existence

They also established, prima facie, that EFG could not be held liable for the plaintiff's injuries because EFG was an out-of-possession landlord that had no duty to remove snow and ice from the subject parking lot
In opposition, the [*2] plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the November 9, 2009 denial of summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: On June 8, 2007, plaintiff allegedly tripped while exiting defendant’s premises and attributed her fall to a crack in a concrete platform step. She described daylight and a clear day with an unobstructed view; the supplied width measurement is garbled.

legal_issues.finding: The crack was shown to be trivial, nonactionable and without trap/nuisance characteristics. Photographs showed slight width and no elevation differential, and testimony established clear daylight and an unobstructed view; plaintiff raised no triable issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff described the crack and conditions, and authenticated photographs. Her numerical width is rendered as “V-k” in the supplied source and is not reconstructed.
Plaintiff confirmed photographs fairly represented the site; they showed slight crack width and no elevation differential.

quality.notes: The bare reference to defendant’s premises does not expressly establish private ownership/control or property use. The bank/company name is not evidence of the accident site’s use. The clear reversal and substantive triviality holding remain recorded. The source’s “V-k” width is preserved exactly and not decoded; OCR does not prevent understanding the holding. other hazard denotes the crack without asserting an elevation difference; stairs_handrail denotes the step, not a handrail issue. Clear daylight and visibility support triviality but are not a separate open-and-obvious ruling. No injured role, legal defendant role, or outside property facts are inferred.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.
On June 8, 2007, a clear, sunny day, the plaintiff was exiting the defendant’s premises when she allegedly tripped and fell. The plaintiff attributed her fall to a crack on a concrete platform step.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Iannacci, J.), entered November 9, 2009, which denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Here, the defendant established, prima facie, that the alleged defect in the step was trivial and nonactionable and did not possess the characteristics of a trap or nuisance

Although the plaintiff, in her deposition testimony, described the width of the crack as V-k inches wide, photographs of the crack, which she confirmed fairly and accurately represented the accident site, indicate that the width was slight and that there was no elevation differential
Further, the plaintiff’s deposition testimony established that the accident occurred during daylight hours on a clear day with nothing obstructing her view
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the November 4, 2015 denial of summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on debris and beer and fell down stairs in the building where she had an apartment. Her daughter reported the condition the prior night and again after the time the superintendent said he had cleaned; plaintiff said she had not left her apartment before falling that day.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant’s superintendent testimony made an initial no-notice showing, but the daughter’s observations of the condition before and after the claimed cleaning raised a triable issue.
The unresolved notice issue also left a triable issue under Multiple Dwelling Law § 80; the court did not conclusively find a statutory violation.
The daughter’s account was not a feigned contradiction because it did not conflict with plaintiff’s testimony that she had not left her apartment before the fall.

evidence_discussed.description: Superintendent described day-specific adherence to cleaning/inspection routines; plaintiff’s daughter testified to the condition’s presence the night before and after the claimed cleaning.
Plaintiff’s deposition stated she had not left her apartment that day before the fall, consistent with the daughter’s separate observations.

quality.notes: Residential use and defendant-associated maintenance are supported, but the generic defendant’s building attribution does not expressly establish private title/control as distinct from a potentially public residential facility. The corporate name alone does not settle private status. other injured role records an apparent resident without inferring a lease/tenancy; other hazard denotes beer rather than calling it water. Defendant’s exact legal role and accident date are unstated. Initial lack-of-notice proof was rebutted; no notice or statutory violation was conclusively found. Cleaning was described in testimony, not records. Private-premises eligibility remains for human review despite the clear substantive affirmance.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Joan A. Madden, J.), entered November 4, 2015, which, in an action for personal injuries sustained when plaintiff slipped and fell down the stairs of defendant's building, denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.
Defendant established entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by showing that it did not have constructive notice of the debris and beer on the stairs on which plaintiff allegedly slipped.

Defendant submitted, inter alia, the testimony of its superintendent, who described his daily cleaning schedule, which included a morning cleaning of the stairs and an evening inspection, and that he adhered to that schedule on the day of the accident

In opposition, plaintiff raised a triable issue of fact through the deposition testimony of her daughter, who testified that the hazardous condition existed the night before the accident, and during the day of the accident, after the superintendent testified that he had cleaned.

since the daughter's testimony did not contradict plaintiff's deposition testimony. In fact, plaintiff stated that on the day of the accident, she did not leave her apartment until the time of her fall.
Contrary to defendant's assertions, this testimony was not "feigned evidence tailored to avoid the consequences of plaintiff's deposition testimony"
Because there is an issue of fact as to notice of the condition, there remains an issue of fact as to whether there is a violation of Multiple Dwelling Law § 80

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the March 18, 2012 order and judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: In December 2008, plaintiff was counting windows to give a cleaning estimate at defendants’ house. While following Papich around its perimeter, she slipped on wet leaves and natural debris on an unimproved slope beside the house, outside any path, walkway or driveway; the record states Papich warned her before the fall.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants established reasonable seasonal maintenance. On this natural non-pathway slope the court found no duty to clear the obvious leaves/debris or warn of the readily observable natural hazard; plaintiff’s opposition did not supply facts imposing such a duty.
The condition resulted from natural seasonal changes, and defendants established noncreation. Plaintiff’s creation claim lacked factual support.
The natural leaf/debris-covered slope was readily observable rather than latent or concealed. The warning duty did not extend to it, and Papich had in any event given a warning.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendants submitted photographs supporting reasonable maintenance and the natural condition; the opinion supplies no individual image descriptions.
Defendants submitted Papich’s and plaintiff’s depositions; plaintiff relied on a deposition excerpt and affidavit in opposition, which failed to raise a triable issue.
Plaintiff also relied on responses to defendants’ bill of particulars, which did not supply facts supporting a clearing duty or creation claim.

quality.notes: Explicit private house ownership and an actual slip support inclusion on natural terrain. other injured role records a prospective window-cleaning service provider giving an estimate without assuming a completed contract or employment. other location preserves the express non-pathway slope; December 2008 remains month/year only. One combined order and judgment is appealed, not two independent rulings. The holding concerns natural geography, reasonable seasonal care and warning duties; it is not a finding that all leaf-covered surfaces are safe or that the hazard lacked inherent danger. No assumption-of-risk or comparative-fault holding is inferred. The warning is uncontroverted but its words are not stated.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order and judgment is affirmed, with costs.

In December 2008, while plaintiff was observing and counting windows in the process of giving defendants an estimate to clean the windows of their house, she reportedly sustained injuries when she slipped and fell while walking with defendant Stanley D. Papich around the perimeter of a house owned by defendants.

Spain, J. Appeal from an order and judgment of the Supreme Court (O’Connor, J.), entered March 18, 2012 in Ulster County, which, granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Plaintiff, following Papich, slipped coming down a slope adjacent to the side of the house that was covered in wet leaves and other natural debris, and thereafter commenced this action, alleging that defendants recklessly maintained the premises, created a dangerous condition and failed to warn her of the dangerous condition.

Defendants satisfied their threshold burden, as the moving parties, by establishing, through photographic evidence and the deposition testimony of Papich and plaintiff, that they exercised reasonable care by maintaining the premises year round and in a seasonally appropriate manner, and that they did not create the condition, which occurred as a result of natural seasonal changes.

Notably, plaintiff’s fall did not occur on a pathway, walkway or driveway but, rather, on the surface of the ground along the side of the house on the unaltered natural contour of the land in an area that was exposed to the elements; it was not foreseeable that someone would traverse on this obviously slippery terrain so as to impose an obligation on the owners to take precautions such as clearing the ground area of leaves and debris

Moreover, defendants’ proof established that the slippery condition of the leaf and debris-covered natural, unimproved downward slope was an open and obvious hazard, as opposed to a latent or concealed one,

While the proof was uncontroverted that Papich did warn plaintiff prior to her fall, the duty to warn *1282 does not extend to open and obvious dangers, particularly those — as here — that encompass “natural geographic phenomena which can be readily observed”
Even viewing the evidence most favorably to plaintiff as the nonmovant, we find that she did not demonstrate a triable issue of fact

In opposing defendants’ motion, plaintiff relied on an excerpt of her deposition testimony, responses to defendants’ bill of particulars and an affidavit, none of which alleged facts from which a duty could be imposed upon defendants to remove from the non-pathway slope the obviously slippery leaves and debris on which plaintiff admittedly slipped. Her claims that defendants created the condition are entirely unsupported by any facts.
Supreme Court granted defendants’ motion, plaintiff now appeals, and we affirm.
